title: Five Classrooms Across Three Thousand Years

zones.label: The Lyceum
zones.tooltip: The Lyceum, about 335 BCE: a research school in a public gymnasium. Click for details.
zones.summary: Aristotle's school was a research school, run by a foreigner in a public gymnasium.
facts: The room: a gymnasium and sanctuary of Apollo Lykeios just outside the eastern walls of Athens. Aristotle founded his school there in 335 BCE.
The teacher: Aristotle was a metic, a free foreigner who could not own land in Athens, so he taught in a public gymnasium where Socrates had talked before him.

The method: not only teaching. Members collected books, plant specimens, and animal descriptions, and compiled the constitutions of 158 states. Only the Constitution of the Athenians survives, recovered on a papyrus published in 1891.
The setback: when Alexander died in 323 BCE, anti-Macedonian feeling turned against his old tutor, and Aristotle left Athens.
Never all the way: Athenian citizenship, and the political life around the school, belonged to adult men born into citizen families. Metics and the enslaved had no political rights.
On our route: the Lyceum site, found in 1996 and opened to visitors in 2014. It is a grid of low foundation walls near the National Garden (Day 13).

zones.label: Rhodes
zones.tooltip: Rhodes, first century BCE: a famous school of rhetoric that learners sailed to. Click for details.
zones.summary: The old pattern of traveling to the teacher: the master's ear could not be carried home.
facts: Locked up: advanced rhetoric lived with a few teachers in a few cities.
Opened: rich Romans could reach those teachers by sea, and the teachers built schools that trained many students at once.

The teaching: Rhodes taught a middle way between the plain Attic style and the ornate Asian style. The most famous teacher was Apollonius Molon. Cicero studied there in 78 to 77 BCE, and by tradition so did Julius Caesar.
Resisted: many Romans distrusted Greek teachers as foreign and corrupting. The Senate expelled Greek philosophers and teachers of rhetoric from Rome in 161 BCE.
Never all the way: only families who could pay for a son's voyage, years abroad, and a Greek tutor ever made the trip, and daughters almost never did.
What a scroll could not carry: an expert who listened, said exactly what was wrong, and made the student do it again, in front of other students.
On our route: Rhodes, Day 8.

zones.label: Aldine Press
zones.tooltip: A Venetian print shop, about 1500: the small, plain, portable book. Click for details.
zones.summary: Aldus Manutius changed the format of the book, and with it the price of owning one.
facts: Locked up: around 1490, to read Plato in Greek in Western Europe a person needed access to a handful of manuscript collections, money to pay a scribe, and a teacher of Greek.
Opened: Aldus's press printed the Greek authors together with the grammars and dictionaries a learner needed. From 1501 his small octavos made the classics something a student could own and carry.
Three choices made the Aldine editions new: the octavo format, a compact italic type cut by Francesco Griffo, and plain texts without thick commentary.
The paper: an octavo sheet makes 16 pages and a folio sheet only 4. In the chapter's illustrative example, one copy of an Aldine-style octavo uses about one-eighth of the paper of the folio.
Resisted: some collectors looked down on print as cheap and common. Aldus himself built a gate, with privileges forbidding others to use his type.
Never all the way: the new books spoke Latin and Greek to men who had been to school. Few women were taught Greek, and most Cretans in the villages could not read at all.
On our route: Heraklion and the Cretan scholars and printers who worked in Venice, Day 9.

zones.label: Medrese
zones.tooltip: An Ottoman medrese, 1550s: free higher education paid for by an endowment. Click for details.
zones.summary: An endowment paid for tuition, room, and meals, so a family's poverty did not decide who could study.
facts: The room: usually a courtyard surrounded by small domed rooms, each a student's cell, with a larger domed classroom on one side. The teachers were called müderris.
Locked up: advanced learning needed years of study that poor families could not afford.

Opened: the endowment of the Süleymaniye külliye (built 1550 to 1557, with four medreses) paid for tuition, a room, meals from the kitchen next door, and a small stipend. Primary schools in mosque complexes taught children of every neighborhood, often girls as well as boys.

Resisted: less by gatekeepers than by inertia. The deeds that kept the schools running made them hard to change, so the curriculum stayed largely what the founders specified while the world moved on to print.
Never all the way: medreses admitted only boys and men, taught in Arabic, and served the empire's Muslim subjects. Christians and Jews ran their own schools through their own communities.
On our route: the Süleymaniye külliye in Istanbul, Day 3.

zones.label: Modern Tutor
zones.tooltip: A learning room today: one-to-one tutoring within reach of every child, with a person in the room. Click for details.
zones.summary: For two thousand years one-to-one attention went to princes. AI tutoring tries to bring it to every child.
facts: Locked up: in 343 BCE Philip II hired Aristotle to teach his thirteen-year-old son Alexander, with a few sons of noble families. For more than two thousand years that advantage went to princes.

The measure: in 1984 Benjamin Bloom reported that the average student tutored with mastery learning scored higher than about 98 percent of a conventional class, a gap of two standard deviations. Tutoring for every child was far too expensive.

Opened, maybe: in a randomized study in a Harvard physics course, students taught by a carefully designed AI tutor learned more, in less time, than students in an active-learning class. A six-week pilot in Edo State, Nigeria, reported gains of about 0.3 standard deviations in English, at very low cost per student.

Resisted, or at risk: other reports describe AI tutors making math mistakes and students using them less than expected, and a study in Turkey shows how an AI helper can harm learning. The evidence is promising and mixed.
Never all the way: children with no connection, no device, or no tutor in their own language are left out first, and they are usually the ones who needed it most.
The picture keeps a person in the room, because the book's closing idea is learning with communities, not to them (Chapters 20 and 21).

quiz.question: Which classroom shows the old pattern of traveling to the teacher, because the master's ear could not be carried home?
quiz.explanation: Cicero sailed for two years and Caesar risked pirates because the best teachers of rhetoric were in a few Greek cities.

quiz.question: In which classroom did the Senate expel Greek teachers of rhetoric from Rome in 161 BCE?
quiz.explanation: Many Romans distrusted Greek teachers as foreign and corrupting. That is the resistance step in Rhodes's story.

quiz.question: Which classroom was a research school that compiled the constitutions of 158 states?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle's school collected books, specimens, and political constitutions. Only the Constitution of the Athenians survives.

quiz.question: In which classroom was the founder a metic, a foreigner who could not own land in the city?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle could not own land in Athens, so he taught in a public gymnasium.

quiz.question: Which classroom cut the cost of owning a classic mainly by changing the format of the book?
quiz.explanation: An octavo sheet makes 16 pages and a folio sheet 4, and paper was among the largest costs of an early printed book.

quiz.question: Which classroom's books spoke Latin and Greek to men who had already been to school?
quiz.explanation: Few women were taught Greek, and most village Cretans could not read at all, so the circle widened but never all the way.

quiz.question: In which classroom did a charitable endowment pay for tuition, a room, meals, and a stipend?
quiz.explanation: The income of the Süleymaniye's endowment paid for the students, so a family's poverty did not decide whether a boy could study.

quiz.question: Which classroom's curriculum stayed largely as its founders specified, while the outside world moved on to print?
quiz.explanation: The deeds that kept the schools running also made them hard to change.

quiz.question: Which classroom tries to bring Bloom's two-standard-deviation tutoring effect to every child?
quiz.explanation: Bloom's tutored students outscored about 98 percent of a conventional class. AI tutoring tries to deliver that attention at the cost of software.

quiz.question: In which classroom are children with no connection, no device, or no tutor in their language left out first?
quiz.explanation: Each classroom widened the circle without reaching everyone, and today's gap is access to a connection, a device, and a tutor in the learner's language.
